file.content:
# 0012: EKS Pod Identity for the upload service

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-19
- **Modules:** upload-service, processor
- **Source:** design doc, section "How the spring boot service pod gets its S3 permissions" (linked from README.md in this folder)

## Decision

The upload service uses EKS Pod Identity. The processor uses data-eng's cross-account IRSA role, which also carries its
SQS and S3 read permissions, so it has one role. The earlier suggestion for the upload service was IRSA; it changed on
19 Oct when infra8's practice became clear.

## Rules for agents

Don't add a role-arn annotation to the upload service's service account, and never put AWS keys in config; the SDK default credential chain picks up the credentials.

# processor configuration

Every `device-logs.*` setting is a field of `config/ProcessorProperties.java`, validated at startup, so a missing or
invalid value stops the pod before it reads the queue. `src/main/resources/application.yml` holds the few defaults; each
environment sets the rest in cloud8-config-service-backend; `application-local-test.yml` holds the LocalStack values.
If this table and the code disagree, the code is right. Change both in the same PR.

## Settings

| Setting | Default in the repo | Local-test value | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `device-logs.aws.region` | none, required | us-west-2 | |
| `device-logs.aws.endpoint-override` | empty | `http://localhost:4566` | LocalStack URL. Empty in AWS. Compose overrides it as `DEVICELOGS_AWS_ENDPOINTOVERRIDE` (see `local/CLAUDE.md`). |
| `device-logs.queue.url` | none, required | `.../000000000000/device-logs-uploads` | |
| `device-logs.queue.visibility-timeout` | none, required (1 s to 12 h) | 60 s | Sent on each receive, so it wins over the queue's own setting. Must be longer than the slowest batch (ADR 0023). |
| `device-logs.queue.max-messages` | 10 | | The most SQS allows per receive. |
| `device-logs.queue.wait-time` | 20 s | | Long-poll wait on an empty queue; the most SQS allows. |
| `device-logs.queue.polling` | true | | Off only in tests that boot the whole app. |
| `device-logs.storage.bucket` | none, required | device-logs-local | The bucket the upload service writes to. |
| `device-logs.index.table` | none, required | device-logs-index | |
| `device-logs.index.retention` | none, required | 30 d | Sets each row's `ttl`. Production value waits on the privacy review (ADR 0008, ADR 0023). |

## Fixed in application.yml

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| `server.port`, `management.server.port` | 1296, 1297 in the jar; 1298, 1299 under `local-test` so it runs next to the upload service |

## Queue settings that are not Java config

Redrive to the DLQ after 5 receives is a property of the queue, set in Terraform in production and in
`local/init/init-aws.sh` locally (ADR 0023). The processor never sends to the DLQ (ADR 0024).

## Credentials

None in config. In the cluster the SDK default chain uses data-eng's cross-account IRSA role, which carries SQS, S3
read and DynamoDB `PutItem` in one role (ADR 0012). The processor has no Helm chart in this repo yet.

content.text:
Neither service puts AWS keys in config. Both build their SDK v2 clients without naming a credentials provider, so the SDK's default credential chain finds the credentials. The difference is which mechanism supplies them in the cluster:

| | Processor | Upload service |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | IRSA, using data-eng's cross-account role | EKS Pod Identity |
| Permissions | One role covering SQS, S3 read and DynamoDB `PutItem` | An IAM role that can write to S3 `raw/*` only |
| Wiring | The processor has no Helm chart in this repo yet | Its own `serviceaccount.yaml` creates the service account with no role-arn annotation. Terraform in infra8 links the role to it by namespace and service account name, so no role ARN appears in the chart or in GDS. |

ADR 0012 says the upload service was first going to use IRSA too. That changed on 19 Oct to follow infra8's practice. The processor stayed on IRSA so all its permissions sit in one role.

In local and integration tests, both services take LocalStack's fake keys from the `aws.accessKeyId` and `aws.secretAccessKey` system properties, which the default chain reads first.
